newsitem.title: UK: Adtranz touts tilting trains for UK trunk railways.
newsitem.headline: Adtranz touts tilting trains for UK trunk railways.

text.p: The British unit of European rail supplier ABB Daimler-Benz Transportation (Adtranz) unveiled its latest family of tilting trains for the UK passenger railway market on Friday, claiming they could cut trunk journey times.

"Adtranz is developing a family of diesel and electric tilting trains specifically for the UK, built on the proven technology of the Swedish X2000 intercity trains and Germany's VT611 inter-regional diesel train," it said in a statement.
Such trains would allow up to 30 percent faster speeds through existing track curves, "significantly reducing journey times" even before infrastructure improvements are carried out.
Seven countries already have tilting train fleets and another eight have them on order, but neither Adtranz nor any of its competitors have broken into the British market.
The company believes the much-maligned West Coast intercity route linking London with Manchester and Glasgow would be an ideal starting point for its marketing efforts.

The line, which is to be upgraded over the next few years in a complex 1.0 billion pound project led by infrastructure owner Railtrack Plc, has contraints due to its twisting tracks, outmoded signalling systems and power restrictions.
Adtranz's plan is to offer its trains ahead of improvements.
John Vale, Adtranz business development manager, told a conference on the future of the West Coast line in Manchester on Friday that new trains soon would make good strategic sense.

A signalling project currently under way involving Siemens, Britain's GEC, Westinghouse and Adtranz is intended to deliver a new signalling system that will permit higher train speeds and more capacity.

"The next step in the strategy needs to be the train. But a train which is already proven and is sufficiently flexible to give immediate benefits whilst able to capitalise on the infrastructure improvements as they are implemented," he said.
Adtranz is making its pitch against the background of this year's total change in Britain's business of train operating.
All the country's 25 passenger operating companies, of which Intercity West Coast is one, are being privatised to franchisees through contracts of seven or more years.

Meanwhile, Railtrack, floated this spring, is evolving a market-based capital raising function for new projects and train builders are looking for customers among either the privatised operators or the three big leasing companies already in place.
A key feature of Vale's paper was his assertion that new trains would lead to immediate revenue benefits at a level comparable to the reduction in journey time.

He said the introduction of the X2000 in Sweden had lifted the market share of rail over air on the trunk route between the main cities of Stockholm and Gothenburg by cutting 25 percent off the rail journey time with only minor track improvements.
Between London and Glasgow, where West Coast trains compete with airlines and the rival East Coast trunk rail line, Adtranz sees potential to cut the journey time from five hours to four.
Adtranz was formed by merging the rail units of Germany's Daimler-Benz AG and Swiss-Swedish ABB.
